prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads moisture levels from a DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 (analog resistive) using an MCP3008 ADC connected on the SPI0 hardware bus, with CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM); the sensor’s analog output is wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0), and the program must sample once per second, logging the raw 10‑bit ADC value (0‑1023) to the console together with a timestamp, while providing robust error handling for any SPI initialization or transfer failures, ensuring that the SPI handle is closed and the driver library is terminated cleanly on all exit paths, and supporting graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the current from an MLX91219 Hall‑Effect Current Sensor (analog output) using an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1, with the sensor’s ADDR pin tied to GND, the sensor’s analog output connected to ADS1115 channel AIN0, SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM); configure the ADS1115 for single‑shot mode, single‑ended input on AIN0 (MUX = 100), a programmable gain of ±4.096 V and a data rate of 128 SPS, then every 500 ms read the 16‑bit conversion result using the appropriate API call with correct byte order, convert it to amperes, and log the current value to the console, while gracefully handling any I2C write or read errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT the program closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY-026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO4 (BCM) and routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0 (single‑ended) while using the MCP3008 chip‑enable CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM); the program must initialize the driver, verify successful SPI open and transfer operations, and on each one‑second interval log a timestamped CSV row containing the current time, a boolean flame‑detected flag derived from the digital line, and an approximated temperature calculated from the analog reading to a file named flame_data.csv, while handling errors by skipping the entry and printing a diagnostic message if the sensor is absent or any SPI or file operation fails, and must ensure all resources are cleanly released on normal exit or when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) as a digital input and an LM393‑based Heat Sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 on I2C bus 1 using channel AIN0 (single‑ended), polling both every 100 ms with a 50 ms debounce applied to the flame sensor, and activates an active‑HIGH buzzer on GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds when both sensors indicate a fire condition at the same time; the program must log a fire event with a timestamp to a file named fire_log.txt when both conditions trigger, log “Flame detected!” if only the flame sensor is active, and log the temperature reading if only the temperature exceeds 60 °C, while performing thorough error handling that checks driver library initialization, I2C opening, ADC configuration writes, ADC reads, and log file creation, printing descriptive error messages to stderr for any failure, releasing any resources acquired so far and exiting with code 1 on any initialization error, and, if an ADC read fails due to I2C error or missing sensor, logging the error and continuing without crashing; the application should handle SIGINT by clearing a running flag so the main loop exits cleanly, and on exit it must turn off the buzzer, deregister any interrupt service routine, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and invoke the driver library’s cleanup call, using only the provided driver library (no other libraries), driving the buzzer with a simple digital write (no PWM), and compiling without warnings under gcc ‑Wall with no undeclared identifiers or implicit declarations.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads the Melexis MLX91219 current sensor (SOIC‑8, –40 °C to 125 °C) through an external MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 CE0 (spidev0.0) configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, sampling once per second, logs each reading with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named current_log.txt, and drives a cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM) HIGH when the measured current exceeds a defined threshold and LOW otherwise; the program must check the result of every open, ioctl, read and write call, detect SPI transfer failures, and treat ADC values of all‑zero or all‑ones as a sensor‑absent condition, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must close the SPI file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, and ensure the fan is turned OFF, using the appropriate driver interface for all GPIO control, opening the GPIO chip by name and attempting the Pi 5 specific API call before falling back to chip 0, and include stdint.h along with any other required standard headers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads a Honeywell/SGX MICROceL MICS-4514 CO sensor (dual‑element MOS, NO2/CO) via I2C bus 1, using an external 16‑bit ADC such as an ADS1115 or a simulated 16‑bit raw reading, converts the raw CO resistance value to a concentration in ppm with a calibrated logarithmic curve, and logs each timestamped ppm value to a file named co_log.txt every 5 seconds; the program must verify successful driver library initialization, creation of the I2C handle, and detect any I2C read failures that indicate a missing sensor or bus error, and it must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY‑026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO 4 (BCM) for flame presence, routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0, and connecting the MCP3008 chip‑select to CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM) with SCLK on GPIO 11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO 10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO 9 (BCM); the program must log once per second to a timestamped CSV file named flame_data.csv containing the flame presence flag (1/0) and a temperature reading, must validate driver library initialization, SPI handle creation, each SPI transfer, and all file I/O, skipping any entry and printing an error to stderr when the sensor is absent or a SPI bus error occurs, and must cleanly release all resources on normal exit and on SIGINT (Ctrl‑C), using the driver library for all GPIO and SPI operations and not employing any other software library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the SGX Sensortech MICS-4514 dual MOS sensor (CO/NO2) over the I2C bus, extracts the two 16‑bit ADC readings (OX for CO and RED for NO2) from the four‑byte response, converts the OX value to a CO concentration in ppm, and every 5 seconds appends the CO ppm value to a file named co_log.txt while also checking whether the value meets or exceeds a 25 ppm alert threshold and, if so, writing an alert entry to a separate file named alert_log.txt; the program must include robust error handling for I2C initialization failures, read errors, and any file‑I/O problems, and must ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, thereby simulating an industrial air‑quality monitoring system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads sound pressure levels from two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU analog MEMS microphones, using a bit‑banged I2C emulation on bus 1 with the analog OUT signals connected to GPIO2/BCM2 and GPIO3/BCM3, samples each microphone every 100 ms, computes the average level, and appends a timestamped entry of that average to a file named audio_log.txt; if a read from either sensor fails the program must log an error value of –999.0 dB for that sample and continue operation, and it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing all I2C handles and terminating the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples audio from two Analog Devices ADMP401 MEMS microphones using an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0, with chip‑select lines CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) and CE1 on GPIO9 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), while driving an LED on GPIO27 (BCM); the program must acquire one sample from each microphone every 1 ms for a total window of 100 ms (100 samples per channel), compute the RMS level for each channel, log the window timestamp together with mic1 RMS and mic2 RMS to a file named audio_events.csv, trigger the LED to stay on for 500 ms whenever either RMS exceeds a high‑level threshold, include error handling for SPI initialization failures and file I/O errors, and cleanly handle a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by turning the LED off and releasing all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples the analog output of a Melexis MLX91204 Hall effect current sensor using an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO2 BCM, SCL on GPIO3 BCM), reading single‑ended on channel A0 at a rate of 10 Hz, converting the raw values to current, storing each converted reading in a circular buffer of 100 elements, and triggering a warning LED on GPIO17 BCM whenever the average of the buffered currents exceeds a 50.0 A threshold; the implementation must employ the driver library I2C API functions for raw register operations, include robust error handling for driver initialization, I2C reads, and sensor‑absent conditions, and handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off the LED and releases all resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Adafruit TCS34725 I2C color sensor on I2C bus 1, initializing the sensor through the supplied driver, waiting at least 3 ms after power‑on before any read, then reading the clear, red, green and blue values once every second and appending a line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,clear,red,green,blue” to a file named color_log.csv, creating the file with a header row if it does not already exist; the program must check the return value of every I2C read and write, printing a warning to stderr on a transient failure and continuing, but if three consecutive I2C operations fail it should exit gracefully, and it must exit with a non‑zero code if the driver initialization or I2C open fails or if the sensor’s ID register does not match the expected value; on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the program must close the I2C handle, flush and close the CSV file, and invoke the driver’s cleanup call, and it must implement the one‑second interval without using a blocking sleep that would prevent signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads analog values from two Seeed Studio Grove Moisture Sensors using an MCP3008 ADC connected on SPI0 via the driver library /dev/spidev0.0, with CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM); sensor 1 is wired to MCP3008 channel 0 and sensor 2 to channel 1, the program must sample both sensors every 5 seconds, log each reading with a timestamp to a file named moisture_log.csv containing the header “Timestamp,Moisture1,Moisture2”, verify that all SPI and driver initialization calls succeed, gracefully handle cases where a sensor is absent or the SPI bus reports an error, and ensure that on any exit path triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM the SPI file descriptors and driver library resources are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Melexis MLX91211 Triaxis Current Sensor (analog ratiometric Hall‑effect) through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0, using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), with the MLX91211 analog output connected to MCP3008 channel 0 and a motor shutdown control on GPIO17 (BCM); the program must sample the current once every second, convert the ADC reading to amperes, write a line containing a timestamp and the current in amperes to a file named current_log.csv (adding a header if the file is new or empty), check all open, ioctl, read and file I/O calls for errors and retry any SPI communication failures up to three times, and implement error handling and graceful termination by catching SIGINT and SIGTERM to close file descriptors and release GPIO lines cleanly; if the measured current exceeds 10.0 A the software must drive GPIO17 low to disable the motor, log the over‑current event, wait one second, then drive GPIO17 high to re‑enable the motor, and continue normal sampling thereafter.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Melexis MLX90817 absolute pressure sensor on I2C bus 1, reading the sensor once per second and appending each measurement to a file named pressure_log.csv that is opened once at startup with a header row and flushed after every write; each CSV line must contain an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp and the pressure in kPa, and the program must check every I2C call and every file operation for errors, printing to stderr the register and the driver error code on any I2C read failure while continuing without logging, handling sensor‑absent conditions such as I2C open failure or repeated read failures, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Melexis MLX90834 pressure sensor (SENT‑only MEMS) through an ADS1115 ADC bridge on the I2C bus, reading the pressure channel on AIN0 and the NTC temperature channel on AIN1 in single‑ended mode, validating every driver call and retrying any failed I2C read up to three times while handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, then printing the pressure in kPa and temperature in °C to the console once per second, driving a warning LED on GPIO17 (active‑high) HIGH whenever the pressure exceeds 105.0 kPa, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads motor current from a Melexis MLX91209 Hall‑effect current sensor (analog output) using an MCP3008 10‑bit SPI ADC on bus SPI0 CE0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, with CE on GPIO8 (BCM), SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), sampling the sensor’s analog output on MCP3008 channel 0 (single‑ended) every 100 ms, logging each reading with a timestamp to a file named current_log.txt in append mode and flushing after every write, handling driver library initialization failures, SPI open or transfer errors, invalid ADC values and file I/O errors, asserting GPIO27 (BCM) HIGH to shut down the motor when the measured current exceeds 10 A, logging an OVERCURRENT event and terminating the program in that case, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly closing the SPI handle, closing the log file, resetting GPIO27 to LOW and invoking the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the analog output of a Honeywell MICROceL MCO‑S4 CO sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 (1 MHz, mode 0) using CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM), SCLK on GPIO 11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO 10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO 9 (BCM), sampling channel 0 once per second, and after each successful read logs the timestamp and voltage to a file named co_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,Voltage: X.XX V”; the program must check the return values of the required library API calls and the SPI transfer function, and if an SPI transfer fails it must log the error, wait one second before retrying, and ensure the alarm connected to GPIO 4 (BCM) is turned off for safety, while under normal operation it drives GPIO 4 HIGH when the measured voltage exceeds 2.5 V and LOW otherwise, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must close the SPI handle, close the log file, turn off the alarm, and invoke the appropriate library cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors methane concentration using a Honeywell MICROpeL Model 41000-020 Combustible Gas Sensor (analog output) interfaced through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI bus 0, channel 0, configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, with VDD/VREF tied to the Pi 3.3 V pin 1, DGND/AGND to any Pi ground, CLK on GPIO11 (SCLK, BCM), DOUT on GPIO9 (MISO, BCM), DIN on GPIO10 (MOSI, BCM) and CS/SHDN on GPIO8 (CE0, BCM); the program must read the sensor once per second, log each reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to “methane_log.txt” in append mode, and write a visible leak alarm to stderr whenever the concentration exceeds 1000 ppm, while checking the library’s API call() three separate times, as well as checking fopen() and localtime_r() for errors, logging any SPI transfer failure to stderr and continuing operation rather than crashing; it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver, and closing any open file handle, and must obey the constraint of not using the driver library directly, instead using the driver’s negative‑handle error codes without invoking the library’s API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads pressure data from a Melexis MLX90830 analog pressure sensor using an ADS1115 16‑bit ADC on I2C bus 1, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM) and the sensor’s analog output wired to ADS1115 channel AIN0, sampling at a rate of 1 Hz, validating that each reading falls within the 0‑100 kPa range, logging each valid pressure value together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt, performing thorough error handling for all I2C and ADC initialization and read operations, detecting and handling conditions such as a missing sensor or bus errors, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when the program receives a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the analog Honeywell HIH-4602-A humidity sensor (which includes an integral thermistor) through an MCP3208 12‑bit ADC connected on the SPI0 bus using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) as the chip‑select line, reads the humidity and temperature values, appends each reading as a comma‑separated line containing a timestamp, humidity, and temperature to a file named humidity_log.txt, and when the humidity value exceeds an 80 % threshold triggers an email alert via ssmtp; the implementation must include robust error handling for the ADC driver initialization, any SPI transfer failures, and all file I/O operations, and must also ensure that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads temperature data from a TMP36 analog temperature sensor using a MCP3208 12‑bit ADC on SPI0 with the device file /dev/spidev0.0 configured for mode 0, 8 bits per word at 1 MHz; the TMP36 signal output is connected to MCP3208 channel 0 (CH0, pin 1), chip‑enable CE0 is on GPIO8 (gpiochip4, BCM), SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO9 (BCM); the MCP3208 VDD and VREF are tied to 3.3 V; the program must perform a conversion at 1 Hz, validate the ADC reading, convert it to a Celsius temperature and log each sample as a line “timestamp,temperature_celsius” to temperature_log.csv, writing a header only when the file is newly created; it must check all SPI open, ioctl and transfer operations for errors, detect sensor‑absent or out‑of‑range conditions (valid range –40 °C to 125 °C), and implement signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully close the SPI device, release the GPIO lines and close the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with an Analog Devices ADXL335 analog accelerometer through an MCP3008 ADC on the SPI0 bus using CE0 (GPIO8) at 1 MHz in mode 0, reading the X axis from MCP3008 channel 0, Y from channel 1, and Z from channel 2, sampling at 100 Hz and logging the raw ADC values for X, Y, and Z to a file named impact_log.txt as timestamped, comma‑separated entries while also writing a line containing “IMPACT DETECTED” to the same log whenever a configurable impact threshold is exceeded; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver, opening of the SPI device, each API call return, and file opening, validate that each ADC read is within the valid range, manage the chip‑select line (GPIO8) correctly around every SPI transfer, and handle a SIGINT signal by cleanly closing the SPI interface, closing the log file, and invoking the appropriate library cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads Heart Rate and SpO₂ data from a Silicon Labs Si1172‑A30‑GMR Optical Heart Rate Sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling once per second, and logs each sample to a file named biometric_log.csv with a header row containing Unix timestamp, HR (bpm), SpO₂ (%), and an error flag (0 = OK, 1 = read error, 2 = sensor absent/uninitialized), flushing the file after every write; the program must check the return value of every driver library I2C call, distinguish transient I2C errors from a completely absent or uninitialized sensor, and when a read fails write a row with the appropriate error flag instead of crashing; because the Si1172 requires a proprietary algorithm to convert raw PPG samples to true HR and SpO₂, the code should log the raw 16‑bit IR and RED ADC values as proxy values for HR and SpO₂ and document this limitation in comments; finally, the application must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, terminates the driver library, and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Honeywell SpiroQuant A+ ES1-005 Mass Flow Sensor (analog output) through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 using mode 0 at 1 MHz on channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8), initializing the driver library and opening the SPI device, then repeatedly reading the ADC, converting the value to a flow rate, validating that the flow rate lies between 0.0 and 5.0 L/min, and logging each measurement once per second with a microsecond‑precision timestamp in the form “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.uuuuuu,flow_rate” to a file named flow_log.csv while flushing the file after every write; the program must check the result of every driver initialization, SPI open, each SPI transfer and each ADC read, treat ADC values of 0 or full‑scale as sensor‑absent conditions, report any out‑of‑range flow rates or other errors to stderr but continue running, and on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—cleanly close the SPI interface, terminate the driver library, and close the log file.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and pressure data from a TDK ICP‑10125 I2C sensor attached to I2C bus 1, issuing the documented high‑precision measurement command, waiting for the conversion, and then reading the 6‑byte result (pressure MSB/LSB, temperature MSB/LSB, CRC bytes) and applying the official ICP‑10125 calibration formulas to convert the raw ADC values to degrees Celsius and pascals; the program must sample every 5 seconds, log each timestamped reading to a file named environmental_data.csv, display the values on the console for real‑time monitoring, check the result of every I2C system call (open, ioctl, write, read) and, on any sensor‑absent or bus‑error condition, log the error and retry after 5 seconds, and finally handle graceful shutdown by catching SIGINT and SIGTERM, closing both the I2C file descriptor and the CSV log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that samples audio simultaneously from two STMicroelectronics MP23ABS1 analog MEMS microphones using an MCP3008 analog‑to‑digital converter connected on SPI0 CE0/GPIO8, applies a basic noise‑cancellation algorithm, and prints the resulting audio samples to the terminal in CSV format; the program must accept gain control values as command‑line arguments, include robust error handling for driver initialization, SPI configuration, and any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and must catch SIGINT to ensure all resources are cleanly released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the analog output of a Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 10‑bit ADC on SPI0 CE0, using channel 0 (CH0) of the ADC, samples the sensor once every 60 seconds in an infinite loop, and appends each measurement to a file named moisture_log.txt as a comma‑separated line containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp and the raw 10‑bit ADC value (0‑1023); the program must verify that all driver initialization and SPI transfer calls succeed, confirm that each reading lies within the valid ADC range, handle any file‑I/O errors gracefully, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly release resources by closing the SPI handle and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the analog voltage from a Keyes KY‑026 Flame Sensor using an MCP3008 ADC connected on the SPI bus /dev/spidev0.0 in mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0) at 1 MHz, with the sensor’s analog output (AO) wired to MCP3008 channel 0, samples the value every 500 ms, performs a 3‑byte SPI transfer (start bit, single‑ended configuration, dummy byte) and, if the transfer fails, logs the error to stderr and to a log file, skips that iteration and ensures the buzzer on GPIO 18 (BCM) is turned OFF for safety; if the returned ADC value is outside the 0‑1023 range, the program retries up to three times before abandoning the iteration; each successful read is temperature‑compensated using the ambient temperature read from a local file ambient_temp.txt (defaulting to 25.0 °C if the file is missing or invalid), and the result is logged to flame_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,raw_adc,voltage,compensated_voltage,temperature,flame_detected”, with the buzzer kept continuously ON while a flame is detected and OFF otherwise; the program must also handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully by stopping the sampling loop, turning the buzzer OFF, closing the log file, and releasing all driver resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the analog output of a DFRobot Gravity Analog Water Level Sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 10‑bit ADC over SPI0 using CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM) with MISO on GPIO 9, MOSI on GPIO 10 and SCLK on GPIO 11 at 1 MHz mode 0 (flags = 0), prints the water‑level percentage to stdout, and appends each reading as a JSON object containing an ISO 8601 timestamp with millisecond precision and the percentage to a file named water_levels.json, maintaining a valid JSON array by writing the opening ‘[’, flushing after each entry, and writing the closing ‘]’ on graceful shutdown; the program must read the sensor every 5 seconds, sleeping in ~100 ms increments via the library’s API call, turn an LED on GPIO 17 (BCM) on when the level exceeds 75 % and off when it falls below 70 % to provide hysteresis, check all return codes on initialization and SPI opening and abort cleanly on failure, handle any SPI transfer errors (negative return from the API call) by reporting the error through the driver library() and skipping that reading without crashing, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM stop the main loop, close the SPI handle, turn off the LED, terminate the driver library, and close the JSON file cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the analog output of a Honeywell AWM7300V mass airflow sensor through an MCP3008 10‑bit ADC connected on SPI0, using CE0 on physical pin 24, SCLK on physical pin 23, MOSI on physical pin 19, and MISO on physical pin 21, with the sensor output wired to MCP3008 channel 0, sampling the flow every 100 milliseconds, converting each sample to Liters Per Minute, and appending a timestamped (ISO 8601) reading to an airflow_log.csv file that includes a CSV header when the file is first created; the program must implement robust error handling for driver initialization, SPI transmission failures, and file I/O errors, and must cleanly release all SPI handles, close the file, and shut down the driver library on every exit path, including graceful termination when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors a potted plant using a HiLetgo Soil Moisture Sensor (analog resistive) connected to the MCP3008 ADC on the SPI bus CE0 (bus 0, channel 0) operating at 500 kHz in single‑ended mode, with the sensor’s analog output wired to MCP3008 channel 0, and logs a timestamped moisture percentage to a file named plant_data.txt in append mode every 60 seconds in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, <moisture_percent>”; the program must accept command‑line arguments to specify the SPI channel, ADC channel, minimum and maximum calibration values, the moisture threshold, the logging interval, the recipient email address, and the path to an msmtp configuration file, must check every initialization call and each SPI transfer for errors printing diagnostics to stderr, must handle a failed ADC read by logging the error to stderr and simply retrying on the next cycle without crashing, must trigger an email alert via msmtp (using popen to pipe the email body, never system with shell interpolation) whenever the measured moisture falls below 30 % (or the user‑supplied threshold), must validate the msmtp exit status, and must cleanly handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver, freeing any dynamically allocated memory and exiting cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors soil moisture using a Keyes KY‑036 analog sensor whose analog output (A0) is wired to the single‑ended channel 0 of an MCP3008 10‑bit SPI ADC; the program must open SPI0 on CE0 (GPIO8) at 1 MHz in mode 0, sample the sensor once per second by default but allow the interval to be overridden by a numeric argument passed as argv[1], and for each reading log a line to soil_moisture.log containing an ISO‑8601 timestamp, the raw 10‑bit ADC value and the calculated moisture percentage, while rigorously checking that the ADC initialization, the SPI device open, every SPI transfer and all file I/O operations succeed, logging a warning and continuing if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs; a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must cleanly close the SPI handle, flush and close the log file, and invoke the ADC’s call() cleanup routine before exiting, and the implementation must read the analog output via the MCP3008 channel 0 without using any driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using the board’s GPIO software PWM bus and four active‑low push‑buttons with internal pull‑ups, where the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), the tilt‑up button to GPIO6 (BCM), the tilt‑down button to GPIO7 (BCM), the pan‑left button to GPIO8 (BCM) and the pan‑right button to GPIO9 (BCM); the program must generate a 50 Hz PWM period (20 ms) with pulse widths ranging from 1 ms to 2 ms (corresponding to duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000), initialize both servos to the mid‑position value 75, and on each button press adjust the corresponding axis by ±5 while clamping the position to the range 25–125, poll the button states every 50 ms, check the return status of every driver call and handle any request failures, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly release all allocated resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running Bookworm 64‑bit that opens the USB camera on /dev/video0, uses select() with a 2‑second timeout to wait for a frame, requests buffers, memory‑maps them, queues a buffer, starts streaming, dequeues the captured frame, stops streaming, unmaps the buffers, frees them and closes the file descriptor, handling SIGINT so that all these steps are performed cleanly on interruption; the captured image, originally in the documented YUYV format, must be converted to RGB24, processed with a blur filter, then encoded as a JPEG file named capture_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg with quality set to 75, and every system call and memory allocation must be checked for failure with error messages printed to stderr and all resources released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running a 32‑bit or 64‑bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active that opens the CSI camera device node /dev/video0, checks that the node exists and can be opened, queries the device capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerates all supported frame sizes using VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES and for each size enumerates the available frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS, then queries the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control with VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL to determine whether autofocus is supported, printing a clear, human‑readable summary of the resolutions, frame rates and autofocus capability to stdout; the program must verify every ioctl return value, handle the cases where the device node is missing, cannot be opened, the camera does not support frame‑size or interval enumeration, or the focus control is absent, and exit with a non‑zero status on any fatal error.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using two hobby servos driven over the GPIO hardware PWM bus, with four active‑low push‑buttons wired to ground and using the internal pull‑up resistors; the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), while the UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT buttons are on GPIO6, GPIO7, GPIO8 and GPIO9 respectively, all using 50 Hz PWM where each loop iteration increments the pulse width by 10 µs and the loop delays 50 ms, the pulse widths must be clamped between 1000 µs (minimum) and 2000 µs (maximum) with a center position of 1500 µs, the program must initialize the driver library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if initialization fails, output a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position, respond to button presses by adjusting the appropriate servo pulse width in the allowed range, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops PWM on both servo pins using the library's API call, calls the library's API call() to release resources, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected on the GPIO bus with its output tied to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11), debounces each motion detection for two seconds, and otherwise polls the pin every 100 ms; when motion is detected the program must capture a JPEG snapshot from the Camera Module v2 at quality 85, store the file in a directory named motion_captures (creating the directory if necessary and handling an existing directory gracefully), then compose a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number and POST this payload together with the image to an HTTP endpoint at http://<IP>:<port>/upload, where the IP address and port are supplied as command‑line arguments; the program must initialize the sensor driver and the HTTP library, configure GPIO17 as an input with a pull‑down resistor, check and report any initialization, system call, file, or network errors to stderr, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a clean shutdown by releasing the driver, performing the required global cleanup of the HTTP library, and exiting, while ensuring the global HTTP library initialization is called exactly once at startup and the corresponding cleanup is called exactly once at exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that monitors the HC‑SR501 PIR sensor on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s output connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) as an input with edge‑falling detection, implements a 50 ms debounce by waiting for a falling edge with a timeout, and upon a valid motion event invokes the camera capture utility with the options ‑o <filename> ‑‑width 640 ‑‑height 480 ‑q 85 ‑‑timeout 2000 ‑‑nopreview to produce a timestamped JPEG saved in /home/pi/images using the filename format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg; each capture and any error from the capture command must be logged with a timestamp to /home/pi/motion_capture.log; the program must open the GPIO chip, claim GPIO17 as an input with edge‑falling (or edge‑rising) detection, check return codes of the capture command and log failures, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all driver library resources and closing file descriptors, while assuming the images directory already exists and avoiding any network publishing, ZeroMQ, or use of a driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32‑bit or 64‑bit) that opens the USB UVC camera on /dev/video0, uses VIDIOC_QUERYCAP to verify the device, configures the capture to the documented V4L2_PIX_FMT_YUYV with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests a single memory‑mapped buffer, starts streaming, and then uses select() with a 2‑second timeout (retrying ioctl calls on EINTR) to wait for a frame; after a successful capture it must check that the returned width, height and pixel format match the requested values before processing, copy the complete YUYV macroblocks (Y0,U,Y1,V) to avoid color corruption, crop a 200 × 150 region, and write exactly 200*150*2 bytes to a file named cropped.yuv, checking the return value of every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen and fwrite and printing any errno with perror followed by EXIT_FAILURE on error; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must cleanly stop streaming, unmap the buffer, close the file descriptor and free any allocated memory.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads arrow‑key presses and a ‘q’ character from stdin, uses the GPIO hardware PWM bus to drive two SG90 servo motors—one pan servo attached to GPIO17 (BCM) and one tilt servo attached to GPIO18 (BCM)—operating at a 50 Hz frequency, initializing the driver library and exiting with code 1 after printing an error if initialization fails, starting both servos at a neutral 90‑degree position, moving each servo in 5‑degree steps in response to the appropriate arrow key while enforcing angle limits of 0 to 180 degrees and printing clear error messages for any out‑of‑range angle or PWM failure, inserting a 100 ms delay between successive commands, and handling cleanup by setting both servos to neutral, terminating the driver library cleanly, and exiting when a SIGINT signal is received or the user presses ‘q’.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and parses the CPU usage percentage from /proc/stat, then renders both values once per second on an SSD1306 128×64 I2C OLED display attached to I2C bus 1, using a basic 5×7 bitmap font for text; the program must check every I2C write operation for errors, handle file‑read failures by returning specific error strings to be shown on the OLED, log any I2C communication failures to stderr and exit gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler to cleanly release all resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the pulse output of a YF‑S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), computes the instantaneous flow rate and accumulates total volume, logs the current flow rate and total volume to the console once every second, and updates an HD44780 LCD attached via I2C bus 1 every ten seconds to display the same current flow rate and accumulated volume; the implementation must include robust error handling for any failures during GPIO initialization and must anticipate and manage possible I2C communication errors, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads an anemometer pulse on GPIO17 (BCM) using an interrupt on the rising edge, counts pulses over a 500 ms sample window to compute real‑time wind speed, and reads wind direction from a wind vane connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0/CE0 in mode 0 at 1 MHz; the program must then update a 16x2 LCD with a PCF8574 backpack on I2C bus 1 to display both wind speed and direction every 500 ms, checking the result of every driver library, I2C and SPI call, detecting sensor‑absent conditions such as the ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023 or any I2C/SPI failures and printing diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run, and finally handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the SPI handle, the I2C handle and any driver library resources, using the provided driver library’s I2C and SPI bit‑bang helpers or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via its spi0SPIOpen call where appropriate.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that measures water flow rate using a single YF‑S201 water flow sensor whose pulse output is connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) and displays the result on an LCD1602 attached via I2C bus 1; the program must count sensor pulses over a 1‑second interval to compute the flow in liters per minute and show “Flow Rate:” on the first line of the LCD and the calculated value formatted as “X.XX L/min” on the second line, while providing robust error handling for driver library initialization, GPIO mode and alert setup, and any I2C bus open or write failures, also detecting and handling sensor‑absent conditions such as zero pulses for extended periods, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path and perform a graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that drives an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix over the GPIO bus, using the row anodes on GPIO 17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM) and the column cathodes on GPIO 5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20 (BCM), scanning each row with an 800 µs delay, lighting an LED by setting the corresponding row HIGH and column LOW, and rendering two wave‑like animations that shift each frame, one moving left‑to‑right and the other right‑to‑left; the program must check every driver call, print descriptive error messages to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status on failure, and must handle a graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing all GPIO lines and performing cleanup, while adhering to the constraint of not using any driver library or deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that creates a wave‑like animation on an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix driven directly over GPIO, with the row anodes connected to GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 (BCM) and the column cathodes to GPIO 14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 (BCM); the program must scan the columns left to right, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW, then for each column set the column cathode LOW and light the LEDs sequentially by setting the corresponding row anodes HIGH, observing a 150 ms delay between columns, checking the result of every GPIO operation and handling a chip‑open failure, using the driver library v2 API for all GPIO calls, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly releases all GPIO lines on exit, while respecting the hardware constraint that each column cathode is wired through a current‑limiting resistor (e.g., 220 Ω) and that a column lights when its cathode is LOW and all row anodes are HIGH, and the program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance measurements for multiple targets from an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time‑of‑Flight multi‑target sensor connected on I2C bus 1, polling the sensor every 100 ms and printing to the console ISO‑8601 timestamped distance values for all detected targets; the program must verify the sensor model ID during initialization, perform the required complex proprietary initialization sequence (or clearly stub the proprietary firmware download with a descriptive comment while keeping the I2C communication and error handling fully implemented), check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT.

static int i2c_write_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    uint8_t buf[2] = { reg, value };
    if (write(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write to reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg16(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint16_t *value) {
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }

        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));

}

static int i2c_write_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    uint8_t buf[2] = { reg, value };
    if (write(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write to reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg16(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint16_t *value) {
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    uint8_t buf[2];
    if (read(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    *value = (uint16_t)buf[0] | ((uint16_t)buf[1] << 8);
    return 0;
}

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a smart parking gate using a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor and a servo motor, connecting the sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/SDA, GPIO3/SCL) with its shutdown line tied to GPIO23 (BCM) and its interrupt line to GPIO24 (BCM), and driving the servo with hardware PWM on GPIO18 (BCM); the program must verify the VL53L1X model ID during initialization, check every I2C read and write for errors, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus fails, open the gate when an object is detected within 50 cm and close it when the distance exceeds 60 cm to provide hysteresis, log each gate state change together with a timestamp and the measured distance to a file named parking_log.txt, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on any exit path by installing SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handlers.

 * Run:    sudo ./gate_control

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor and controls a DC motor on GPIO17 (forward) and GPIO18 (backward) according to distance thresholds, triggering a distance reading on each rising edge of GPIO24 (BCM) via a pigpio ISR, where distances below 100 mm cause the motor to run forward, distances above 300 mm cause it to run backward, and values in between stop the motor, while logging every distance measurement and any motor state change to the console; the program must perform the VL53L1X register sequence of a soft reset write, a 1 ms delay, a start‑measurement write, then poll the status register until the data‑ready bit is set before reading the 16‑bit distance value, must check all driver and I2C return values, retry failed I2C transactions with exponential backoff, safely stop the motor if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly release resources by closing I2C handles, stopping the motor, and invoking the sensor’s API cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a proximity‑based interactive art installation using an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor connected on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2/SDA and GPIO 3/SCL); the program must poll the touch status registers every 50 ms, monitor all twelve electrodes (ELE0‑ELE11), and when any electrode detects proximity it should drive a distinct 4‑bit LED pattern on GPIO 17 (BCM) as bit 0, GPIO 18 as bit 1, GPIO 27 as bit 2, and GPIO 22 as bit 3, while logging every proximity event to the console with a timestamp; it must validate every I2C read and write, verify the sensor is present by reading back a known register after a soft reset, and gracefully handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and finally ensure clean resource release on all exit paths by releasing all GPIO lines, closing the I2C and log file descriptors, and installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a capacitive touch‑based proximity detector using an MPR121 connected on I2C bus 1, reads the device ID to verify the sensor is present, configures all required MPR121 registers including FFI, SFI, ESI, debounce, AFE configuration and baseline filtering, monitors the touch inputs for a proximity event, and when such an event is detected turns an LED wired to GPIO 27 (BCM numbering) on for exactly one second, logs the proximity event with a timestamp to a file named proximity.log, handles any I2C communication errors gracefully, and ensures that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that measures distance using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus with the trigger line wired to GPIO17 (BCM, output) and the echo line to GPIO18 (BCM, input); the program must hold the trigger low for 5 µs, then pulse it high for 10 µs before returning it low, wait up to 30 ms for the echo rising edge, then measure the echo pulse width with a further 30 ms timeout, compute distance using the speed of sound ≈ 343 m/s at 20 °C, reject any reading outside the 2‑400 cm range and log an error line instead, and otherwise write a line to a file named distance_log.txt every second containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp and the measured distance, flushing after each write; each access to the trigger and echo pins must include proper error checking, sensor‑absent conditions (echo never rises) and timeout paths must be handled explicitly, a SIGINT handler must be installed that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, and on receipt of SIGINT the program must release all driver resources, close the log file and exit cleanly without leaking resources on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that measures distance with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor using an interrupt‑driven echo pulse‑width measurement on the GPIO bus, with TRIG connected to GPIO17 (BCM) and ECHO connected to GPIO18 (BCM) through a 1 kΩ/2 kΩ voltage divider to keep the Pi input at ~3.3 V, generating a 10 µs trigger pulse once per second, capturing the echo pulse width via an ISR callback on either‑edge transitions, validating that the pulse width is greater than zero and falls within a sane range (approximately 58 µs to 25 ms, corresponding to about 1 cm to 4 m) while handling tick wrap‑around, converting the measured time to meters, and appending each reading together with a timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt; the program must check that the driver library initializes correctly and that the log file opens successfully, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly shuts down by disabling the ISR, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call, with no use of UDP networking or any other external communication.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, controls the sensor’s XSHUT pin with GPIO27 (BCM) configured as an output and set high to enable the sensor (active‑low trigger), repeatedly reads the distance every 100 ms, and logs each reading to the systemd journal via syslog including a timestamp, the measured distance in millimetres, and the sensor status, using LOG_INFO for successful reads and LOG_ERR for any read failures; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the I2C device can be opened, handle read errors by logging them and continuing the loop without crashing, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the I2C handle, terminate the driver library, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) to poll distance measurements every 100 ms, converts the 16‑bit register value from millimetres to centimetres, and controls a gate actuator connected to GPIO24 (BCM, active‑high) so that the gate is opened when the measured distance is less than 20 cm and closed otherwise, initializing the gate to the closed state (GPIO24 low) at startup; the program must log each distance reading, each gate state change, and any errors with timestamps to a file named “gate_log.txt”, perform error handling for all I2C operations, sensor initialization, and file operations, and include a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that gracefully shuts down by closing the I2C interface, closing the log file, and terminating the driver library.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor and drives an 8‑ohm speaker as a theremin‑like instrument, using the hardware‑timed PWM on PWM0 (GPIO18, BCM) to generate audio tones whose pitch is controlled by the measured distance; the HC‑SR04 trigger line must be pulsed for 10 µs on GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line read on GPIO24 (BCM) with a timeout of 200 ms, mapping distances from 2 cm to 200 cm to frequencies between 200 Hz and 2000 Hz on a logarithmic scale with a 50 % duty cycle, while performing robust error checking on every driver API call and, if a distance is out of range or a timeout occurs, preserving the previous frequency, and installing a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops the PWM and terminates the driver, ensuring all resources are released on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that synthesizes a theremin‑like instrument using a piezo buzzer whose pitch is controlled by the distance measured with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor; the buzzer is connected to PWM0 on GPIO18 (BCM), the HC‑SR04 trigger line to GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line to GPIO24 (BCM) with a pull‑down resistor, and the program must initialize the driver library, verify that the GPIO modes are correctly set, then in a loop trigger the sensor with a low‑initial state followed by a 10 µs high pulse, measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using the library’s timing API, enforce an echo timeout of 100 ms (reporting an error and reusing the last valid distance if exceeded), wait 10 ms between readings, map the practical distance range of 5 cm to 50 cm linearly to a frequency range of 200 Hz to 2000 Hz (clamping outside values), generate a continuous tone on the buzzer using the library’s frequency generation API (not raw PWM), print both the measured distance and the resulting frequency to the console each iteration, handle any sensor read failures gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler that stops the PWM and shuts down the driver library cleanly on program termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously measures the distance to the nearest object using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor, triggering the sensor on GPIO17 (BCM) with a 10 µs pulse and reading the echo on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 50 ms timeout, looping every 500 ms; the program must initialise the driver library, configure the trigger pin as an output initially low and the echo pin as an input, check that the driver library initialisation succeeds, obtain each echo pulse duration, convert it to a distance in centimeters, reject any reading below 2 cm or above 400 cm and print “Invalid reading” for those, otherwise print the valid distance as “Distance: X.XX cm”, and if the distance is below 10 cm also print “Too close!”; it must handle a timeout from the echo measurement by treating it as a –1 result, and it must install a SIGINT handler that sets a flag to exit the loop, then terminates the driver library and releases all resources before exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic time‑of‑flight sensor over SPI (mode 0, 1 MHz clock) using the chip‑select line on GPIO8 (BCM, CE0), continuously reads the distance for an obstacle‑avoidance application with a 100 ms delay between readings, and appends each timestamp and distance value in millimetres (range 200‑5000 mm) to a file named distance_log.csv opened in append mode; the program must use the sensor driver’s API call for SPI read operations, handle SPI communication errors, sensor initialization failures, and sensor‑absent conditions gracefully by logging errors to stderr while continuing to run indefinitely, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the SPI handle, releases all resources, and flushes and closes the CSV log file on exit.

 * Build: gcc -O2 -Wall -o icu20201_tof icu20201_tof.c

#include <stdio.h>

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from an Analog Devices TMP05 digital temperature sensor by polling its PWM‑style output on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), measuring the high‑pulse width and total cycle width with a busy‑wait loop using microsecond‑resolution timestamps obtained from the library’s call() API, sampling once every 5 seconds and applying a 50 ms timeout on each edge wait; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the log file “temperature_log.txt” opens in append mode, compute the temperature while guarding against division by zero if the low‑time (TL) is zero, flag any reading outside the valid range of –40 °C to +150 °C as an error, and after three consecutive failures write a “SENSOR MALFUNCTION” entry to the log, logging each valid reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by closing the file and releasing the driver library resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35‑DIS‑B sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented high‑repeatability, clock‑stretching‑disabled measurement command, validates the 8‑bit CRC for both the temperature and humidity words, and, after waiting at least 15 ms for the 6‑byte result, converts the raw values to degrees Celsius and percent relative humidity with the standard Sensirion formulas, then adds a sinusoidal offset of ±2 °C and ±5 % RH over a one‑hour period to simulate a greenhouse environment before logging each reading with an ISO‑8601 UTC timestamp to a file named “environmental_data.txt” every 5 seconds; if any I2C read/write or CRC check fails, the program must retry up to three times with a one‑second delay and, after exhausting retries, log NaN values, while also providing robust error handling for driver initialization, I2C open/read/write, and file open, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating the driver cleanly.

 * Build:
 *   gcc -O2 -Wall -o sdp32_reader sdp32_reader.c
 *
 * Usage:
 *   ./sdp32_reader [interval_ms]
 *

 *   interval_ms = 1000 (1 second)

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the absolute pressure and temperature from a Melexis MLX90824 absolute pressure sensor over the I2C bus, performing a read cycle every 2 seconds, and appends each measurement together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt; the program must check the result of every driver library or I2C call, and if the sensor is absent, the bus reports an error, or a read fails, it must log the error with a timestamp instead of silently skipping, and it must ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, SIGINT, and SIGTERM—it cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the sensor library’s cleanup API, while running indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the temperature from an STMicroelectronics LM75B sensor on the I2C bus once every second, stores the last 60 samples in a circular buffer in memory, computes the running average, and drives a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan is turned on when the average exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off when it falls below 26.0 °C; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, opening of the I2C interface, each I2C read, and each GPIO write, logging any failures to stderr and simply retrying on the next cycle without crashing, and it must handle SIGINT or SIGTERM by stopping the fan, closing the I2C handle, and terminating the driver library cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C, waiting 45 ms after issuing the first measurement command before reading, then sampling once every second, reading exactly nine bytes each cycle and validating each CRC using the Sensirion CRC‑8 polynomial and its documented initial value; the program must log each reading to a file named airflow.log in CSV format with columns timestamp, differential pressure (Pa) and temperature (°C), print a warning to stderr whenever the pressure exceeds 5.0 Pa, robustly handle I2C read/write failures, CRC mismatches and the case where the sensor is absent, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle, close the log file and invoke the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from an STTS2004 temperature sensor on the I2C bus, logs the temperature to stdout once per second, and drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the LED is set high when the temperature exceeds 28 °C and low when it falls below 27 °C; the program must check the result of every I2C read and every GPIO operation, and on repeated I2C failures it must log the errno details and exit cleanly, while handling SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all driver library resources, closing the I2C file descriptor, turning the LED off, and then exiting.
pinned_library: Linux i2c-dev for I2C access, libgpiod for GPIO/LED control

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 45 ms after initiating a measurement before reading the result, retrieving exactly nine bytes consisting of two bytes of differential pressure followed by a CRC byte, two bytes of temperature followed by a CRC byte, and three bytes of scale‑factor data, validating each CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial and initialization value, logging the measured values with timestamps to a file named flow_data.txt, handling any I2C communication errors or the sensor‑absent condition gracefully, and ensuring that all resources are released on every exit path by installing a signal handler for SIGINT that performs the required cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor on the I2C bus using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM, bus 1 default) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM, bus 1 default), waiting at least 20 ms after issuing a no‑hold command and sampling every 60 seconds, logging each reading to a file named environment.log in CSV format with columns timestamp, temperature_c, humidity_pct while also printing the same line to stdout, handling errors by retrying each I2C transaction up to three times, validating sensor presence at startup by reading its electronic ID or firmware revision and exiting with a non‑zero status after logging a timestamped error to both the log file and stderr if the sensor is absent, flushing the log after every write, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call, while using the “Measure Relative Humidity, No Master Hold” and “Measure Temperature, No Master Hold” commands or alternatively the “Read Temperature from Previous RH Measurement” command and performing raw byte transfers rather than register‑addressed reads.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a TI HDC1080 sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 20 ms after each trigger to allow conversion, and appends a line to enviro_log.txt every 5 seconds in the format “timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent”; the program must initialize the driver and open the I2C bus with error checking, gracefully handle any I2C communication failures or a missing sensor by skipping the log entry on error, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle and terminate the driver, running in an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the temperature from a Sensirion STS40 I2C temperature sensor on the I2C bus, waiting 10 ms after each trigger for the conversion to complete and sampling the value every 5 seconds, logging each reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named temperature_log.txt; the program must open the I2C device with open(), set the slave address using ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read exactly three bytes (two data bytes and one CRC8 byte), verify the CRC8 using the Sensirion‑specified polynomial, and on any error condition—including failures to open the device, ioctl, read, write, CRC mismatch, or open the log file—print a descriptive message to stderr and then continue looping; it must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting, and run indefinitely in an infinite loop.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors air‑duct pressure in a simulated HVAC system using the Sensirion SDP810‑500Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus, triggering a measurement, waiting at least 50 ms, then reading the 9‑byte result (2 bytes pressure, 1 byte CRC, 2 bytes temperature, 1 byte CRC, 3 bytes scale factor) once per second, validating every I2C read and write as well as each CRC‑8 using the polynomial and initial value documented for the sensor, logging each successful sample to a file named hvac_pressure_log.txt in CSV format with columns timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C, and on any I2C or CRC error writing an error line with the timestamp and continuing, checking the return of every initialization call (the two required library API calls and fopen) and exiting with an error message if any fails, and handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and calling the library’s cleanup API function before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that drives a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C, buffers CO₂, temperature and humidity readings in a thread‑safe circular buffer of capacity 100, and periodically persists the data to a timestamped CSV file in /var/log/scd40_data/ (creating the directory if it does not exist) with a header row, while logging any errors with timestamps to /var/log/scd40_error.log; the main loop must wait at least one second after issuing the start‑periodic‑measurement command before the first read, then read the sensor every five seconds, validating the CRC‑8 of each value using the polynomial and initial value documented for the device and, on any CRC failure or I2C read/write error, log the error and skip that reading; a separate logging thread must write the buffered records to the CSV file every sixty seconds, and the program must handle SIGINT by using a volatile sig_atomic_t running flag to stop the main loop, send the documented stop‑periodic‑measurement command, join the logging thread, flush any remaining buffered data to a final CSV file, close the I2C handle and cleanly terminate the driver without any resource leaks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1, assuming the sensors are attached through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout or a comparable I2C hub, and polls each sensor once per second, reading three bytes from each (two data bytes followed by a CRC‑8 byte) while validating the checksum and retrying up to three times on any I2C error before giving up on that read; when a valid reading is obtained, the program must append a line to flow_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2”, skipping the entry if the CRC check fails, and it must handle a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by closing all I2C handles and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall‑Effect latch sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with Channel A wired to GPIO17 and Channel B to GPIO18, configuring the pins as open‑drain outputs with internal pull‑up resistors enabled, implementing a 2‑bit quadrature state machine that resolves 360 pulses per revolution into a normalized angular position ranging from 0.00 to 360.00 degrees, logging each timestamped position change to a file named encoder_log.txt, providing robust error handling for both GPIO initialization and file I/O operations, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal by using the driver library’s cleanup facilities.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and logs each measurement to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt with columns timestamp, red, and ir; the program must also monitor the infrared reading and activate an LED connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the IR value exceeds a threshold of 2000, while robustly handling I2C read/write errors and conditions where the sensor is absent, and it must cleanly release all resources—including the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and the log file—on any exit path by catching SIGINT and SIGTERM signals for graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90254 magnetic speed sensor by counting its pulses on the GPIO bus, using GPIO18 (physical pin 12) configured as an input with a pull‑down resistor, counting only rising edges and assuming one pulse per revolution; the program must calculate the RPM over a 1‑second interval, protect the pulse counter with a pthread mutex shared between the interrupt service routine and the main thread, log each RPM value together with a timestamp to rpm_log.txt in append mode flushing the file immediately, include error handling that checks the driver library initialization, ISR registration, and log file opening, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by terminating the driver library, closing the log file, and destroying the mutex, while also handling the case of a missing sensor by logging 0.00 RPM when no pulses are detected.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that communicates over I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, logs each timestamped reading to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt, and triggers an LED connected to GPIO17 whenever the infrared reading exceeds a threshold of 2000; the implementation must robustly handle I2C errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and must clean up all resources—including the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and the log file—on every exit path, also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, while avoiding any use of deprecated driver libraries or driver library components.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that samples the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier connected via GPIO, using the OUT pin (audio signal) on GPIO17 as an input and the GAIN select pin on GPIO18 as an output (set GPIO18 LOW to select 60 dB gain), polls the digital input every 10 ms to rapidly detect rising edges that indicate peak sound events, logs each detected event to a file named audio_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL” where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge, prints a startup message, and runs indefinitely until interrupted, while handling all driver library initialization and I/O errors robustly by checking the return value of every API call and ensuring clean release of all driver library resources on all exit paths through SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the flow rate of a microfluidic drug delivery system using a Sensirion SLF3S‑4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected to I2C bus 1, reading the sensor every 1000 ms by retrieving three bytes (a two‑byte MSB‑first raw value followed by a CRC‑8 byte that must be validated with the documented polynomial and initial value), logging each successful measurement to a CSV file named flow_log.csv in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min” with the file opened once at startup in append mode, kept open, and flushed after each write; the program must check driver initialization, I2C open, write, and read operations, log any I2C read/write failures to stderr and attempt recovery on the next loop iteration, log a CRC failure as an error and skip that reading, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Honeywell MICS‑VZ‑89TE VOC sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the sensor data, computes an indoor air quality (IAQ) index, and logs a timestamped line every 5 seconds to a CSV file named air_quality_log.csv containing the IAQ value together with TVOC in ppb and eCO₂ in ppm; the implementation must check every I2C read and write return value, detect and handle conditions where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error without crashing, and must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt gracefully closes the I2C interface, flushes and closes the log file, and terminates the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line wired to GPIO 17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) as an input with the consumer label “ttp223_tamper”, polling the line every 100 ms based on CLOCK_MONOTONIC; the program must detect when the TTP223B output, which is HIGH while touched and LOW when released, remains continuously HIGH for more than 5 seconds, then print a single intrusion alert to stdout for that touch event and reset the timer when the sensor is released so that alerts are not repeated for the same touch, while checking every library call for failure and printing strerror(errno) on error, and if a sensor read fails mid‑loop printing an error and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE after performing cleanup; the cleanup routine must also be invoked on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM to gracefully release the line and close the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously samples audio from an InvenSense INMP441 I2S MEMS microphone over the I2S bus using the Linux ALSA subsystem (e.g., /dev/snd/pcmC0D0c) and writes the 16‑bit PCM samples to a raw file named audio_capture.pcm, while driving the L/R channel‑select line on GPIO 17 (BCM) to select the left channel, and includes robust handling of I2S initialization failures, data acquisition errors, and file I/O problems together with proper resource release on all exit paths, including graceful termination when receiving a SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a SainSmart IR Flame Sensor Module (LM393 comparator with IR photodiode) connected via GPIO, reading the digital output (DO) on GPIO4 (BCM) every 50 ms and applying a 50 ms software debounce, and when the sensor output goes LOW indicating a flame, immediately start a hardware PWM signal at 100 Hz on GPIO18 (BCM) to drive a cooling fan, logging each event to a file named flame_log.txt with ISO‑8601 timestamps for system start, flame detection, flame end, and program shutdown; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, check the result of every GPIO read, detect a sensor‑absent condition by timing out if no valid reading is obtained, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly stop the PWM, reset the GPIO pins, terminate the driver library, and close the log file.
