prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads flow rates from two Sensirion SLF3S‑0600F Liquid Flow Sensors connected on I2C (/dev/i2c‑1) and logs the average flow rate to a file named flow_log.txt every second, while also driving an alarm on GPIO17 (BCM) when the average of the valid sensor readings falls below 0.5 ml/min and keeping the alarm low otherwise; after issuing a start command to each sensor the program must wait 100 ms before taking the first measurement, then perform subsequent reads at 1‑second intervals, validating each measurement with the Sensirion 8‑bit CRC using the documented polynomial and initial value, and on any I2C communication error or CRC failure it must log the error and skip that sensor’s reading for that cycle, and finally it must handle a clean shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by releasing the GPIO line, closing the I2C file descriptor and the log file.
pinned_library: libgpiod (GPIO) and Linux I2C character-device API (i2c-dev ioctl on /dev/i2c-1)

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously polls a KY-033 Obstacle Avoidance Sensor Module connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor output on GPIO4 (BCM pin 7) configured as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled, sampling every 50 ms; the program must initialize the driver library and verify success, printing an error to stderr and returning a non‑zero code if initialization fails, record each detection (the sensor drives the line LOW when an obstacle is within the threshold and HIGH otherwise) in a circular buffer of 100 entries overwriting the oldest when full, emit an alert to stdout on every detection, and on receipt of SIGINT release all driver resources, then dump the entire buffer in chronological order to stdout with human‑readable timestamps before exiting cleanly, while ensuring no deprecated APIs are used.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 running the 64‑bit Bookworm OS that interfaces with an Omron D7S vibration sensor over I2C (/dev/i2c-1) using GPIO2 (BCM) for SDA and GPIO3 (BCM) for SCL at up to 400 kHz, switches the sensor to the appropriate mode and then waits up to one second for it to become active, after which it polls the acceleration registers every 500 ms to obtain X, Y and Z values, appends each sample to a CSV file named fan_health.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and a header row written only when the file is newly created, checks the return value of every I2C system call and, on any read, write or ioctl failure, prints a diagnostic message to stderr and simply retries on the next loop iteration without crashing, aborts with an error message and exit if the sensor does not become active within the one‑second window, and handles SIGINT and SIGTERM by cleanly closing the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file before exiting, running continuously until interrupted by the user.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces two Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors on the GPIO bus, connecting sensor 1 OUT to GPIO23 (BCM), sensor 2 OUT to GPIO24 (BCM), and driving an LED (anode) on GPIO25 (BCM) through a 220‑330 Ω resistor to ground, polling the sensor outputs every 100 ms, turning the LED on immediately when either sensor reads LOW (active‑LOW indicating an obstacle within roughly 10 cm) and turning it off only when both sensors read HIGH, verifying the driver initialization and checking the return code of every library API call, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released via the appropriate library call on every exit path, including handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a conveyor belt using two E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensors connected via GPIO, with sensor 1 OUT wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 OUT wired to GPIO18 (BCM); the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, validate each sensor read, and consider a stall confirmed only when both sensors read LOW (0) continuously for at least 2 seconds, then record a timestamped entry for each confirmed stall in a file named stall_log.txt while avoiding duplicate entries for the same stall event, handling any file I/O errors that may occur, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the process receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with the Texas Instruments TMAG5170‑Q1 I2C 3D Hall‑Effect sensor on I2C bus 1, configures the sensor for continuous‑conversion mode with all three axes enabled and a 50 mT range, then reads the X, Y, and Z magnetic field values every 100 ms in an infinite loop until the user terminates the program with Ctrl‑C, logging each reading to a CSV file named magnetic_log.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and writing a header row if the file is newly created, while checking every I2C read and write return code and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions by printing error messages to stderr and continuing operation, and finally registering a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the CSV file, and invoking the sensor’s library cleanup call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that runs as a daemon and continuously polls the SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to the GPIO bus on pin GPIO23 (BCM numbering), using a pull‑down resistor on the input to keep the line low when dry, reading the sensor every 2 seconds and generating an alert whenever a logic HIGH is detected; on each detection the program must print an alert message to stdout and append a line to a file named flood_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected”, while also checking that the driver library initializes correctly and, if a GPIO read fails, logging an error entry to the same file and scheduling an automatic re‑initialization attempt after 60 seconds; the daemon must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to release all resources cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Bookworm or later that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall‑effect sensor connected to the GPIO bus, with the sensor output wired to physical pin 7 (BCM GPIO4), by configuring the pin as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled and counting rising‑edge pulses using GPIO interrupts; the program must count pulses in a one‑second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, compute the revolutions per minute, and log one sample per second to a file named rpm_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>” while also printing the same line to stdout, flushing the file after each write; it must check every driver‑library call and the file‑open call for errors, exiting with a diagnostic message on failure, but if the sensor is absent or not rotating it should log an RPM of 0 instead of aborting; finally, the program must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall‑effect sensors connected on the GPIO bus in an interrupt‑driven quadrature configuration, with Sensor A wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and Sensor B to GPIO27 (BCM) and hardware pull‑up resistors providing the required 90° electrical offset, to detect the direction of rotation and log each clockwise or counter‑clockwise event to a file named rotation_log.txt using millisecond‑precision timestamps formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.mmm”; the implementation must employ the driver’s edge‑triggered alerts via the library’s API call for interrupt handling (without using any other driver library), maintain a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to infer direction, protect the shared state between the ISR and the main thread with a mutex, have the main loop wait on a condition variable or sleep rather than busy‑wait, check all error paths including each of the three library’s API call() invocations and the file open operation, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by flushing and closing the log file and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the GPIO bus to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B digital capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO23 (physical pin 16, BCM 23) and to drive an LED on GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18) with an appropriate current‑limiting resistor, polling the sensor every 50 ms so that the LED is illuminated only while the sensor is actively touched; the program must open the GPIO chip, request the input line for the sensor and the output line for the LED, check the return status of every driver call including chip opening, line requests, reads and writes, handle the situation where the GPIO chip is unavailable, log startup, shutdown, each touch event and any errors to the system syslog using openlog/syslog, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that perform a graceful shutdown by turning the LED off and releasing all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads touch input from a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) to capture rising‑edge events and toggles an LED attached to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) on each detected touch; the program must employ the line event interface to wait for rising edges rather than polling, apply a software debounce of approximately 50 ms after each rising‑edge detection, initialize the LED line as an output and drive it LOW at startup, verify the result of every driver call (chip open, line request, event wait, read, write) and print clear error messages to stderr when a call fails, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by gracefully releasing all driver resources (lines and chip) before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls two SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensors on the GPIO bus—sensor 1 connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO17 (BCM)—with a 50 ms loop to debounce, drives LED 1 on GPIO27 (BCM) and LED 2 on GPIO22 (BCM) such that each LED is lit while its corresponding sensor is touched (sensors are active‑high digital outputs), records every touch and release event in a 100‑entry in‑RAM circular buffer storing the sensor pin number, a Unix timestamp, and the new state while maintaining an overflow counter, checks the return value of every API call and prints a diagnostic to stderr on any failure, handles SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off both LEDs, calls the required API cleanup function, and on shutdown prints the full contents of the log buffer together with the overflow count to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a Raindrop Sensor Module with a digital output connected to GPIO17 (BCM) on the GPIO bus, enabling the internal pull‑up resistor on that pin so the input is defined when the sensor is disconnected, and polls the pin every 500 ms; the program must detect the active‑low condition where a LOW (0) level indicates rain and a HIGH (1) level indicates no rain, and it should write timestamped “Rain Detected” or “No Rain” messages to /var/log/rain_events.log only when the state changes, while checking the return value of every driver library call and of fopen, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the log file and releases any driver resources on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors a rotating shaft’s RPM by reading two DRV5032FJDBZR Hall‑Effect sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO18 (BCM), applying approximately a 5 ms debounce to each state change, logging every transition to a CSV file named shaft_log.txt in the format “timestamp,sensor1_state,sensor2_state”, printing the calculated RPM to the console, handling any GPIO initialization failures or file I/O errors gracefully, including the standard headers such as errno.h and string.h to ensure clean compilation, and guaranteeing that all resources are released properly on every exit path, including handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform orderly cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads heart rate and SpO2 data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 I2C optical sensor on I2C bus 1, pausing one second between each read, and appends each measurement to a file named biometric_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Heart Rate: X BPM, SpO2: Y%%” while flushing the file after every write; the program must use the driver library for I2C access, check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, print any communication errors to stderr and keep running, and it must also install a SIGINT handler so that when Ctrl‑C is pressed it gracefully shuts down by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and terminating the driver library before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the structural integrity of a miniature bridge model using two digital tilt sensors (Omron D7E-3) connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 on GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 on GPIO18 (BCM), both configured as inputs with internal pull‑down resistors enabled, and drives an alarm (buzzer/LED) on GPIO27 (BCM) which is active‑high and initialized LOW; the program must poll each sensor every 100 ms via the library’s API call, log ISO‑8601 timestamps (YYYY‑MM‑DDTHH:MM:SS) to a file named bridge_integrity.log for tilt‑start, threshold‑exceeded, and tilt‑end events, activate the alarm if either sensor reads HIGH continuously for more than 2 seconds, deactivate the alarm when both sensors return to LOW, include error handling that checks the driver library initialization, the log file opening, and the API call return values, and implement clean shutdown handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivates the alarm, closes the log file, calls the library’s API cleanup, and guarantees the alarm is off on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an Omron D7S‑A0011 seismic sensor on I2C bus 1 using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), polls the sensor every 100 ms, detects earthquake‑like events when the Euclidean vibration magnitude exceeds a threshold of 500, logs each threshold‑exceeding event to a file named seismic_events.log with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the peak vibration value, turns on an alert LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for 1 second for each such event, initializes the sensor by verifying its presence and clearing the power‑down bit in CTRL1, handles I2C communication errors and sensor‑absent conditions with up to three retries per read, and on receipt of Ctrl+C/SIGINT cleanly releases the I2C handle, the driver library, and closes the log file; the program must be built with gcc -O2 -Wall -o seismic seismic.c -lthe driver library -lm -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements an adaptive grow light system using a VEML7700 lux sensor on I2C bus 1 to set the brightness of a grow light LED connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hardware PWM at a 1000 Hz frequency, sampling the ambient light every 1 second, mapping lux readings to PWM duty cycles in the range 0‑100 according to the rule lux < 100 → 100 % brightness, lux < 500 → 75 %, lux < 1000 → 50 %, lux ≥ 1000 → 25 %, writing a line to “grow_log.txt” after each sample that contains an ISO‑8601 timestamp, the measured lux value, the selected brightness level, and an error code, flushing the file after each write, checking and handling errors for driver initialization, opening the I2C bus, configuring the sensor, reading the ambient light sensor, and performing PWM operations, logging and handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus fails, and providing a graceful shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM that turns off the LED, closes the I2C bus, closes the log file, and terminates the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an 8‑channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module over GPIO, reading channels 1‑8 on BCM pins 2‑9 (configured as inputs with pull‑down resistors) and controlling an alert LED on BCM GPIO17 (configured as an output); the program must initialize the driver library and verify success, exiting with an error message on failure, then poll the sensor every 50 ms, debounce each channel so that a single press generates only one log entry, write each touch event to a file named touch_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS – Channel X Touched” (where X is 1‑8), ensure all file I/O operations are checked for errors with diagnostics printed to stderr, turn the LED on whenever any channel transitions from untouched to touched and turn it off only when all channels are released, and install a clean signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turns off the LED, releases the driver library resources, and exits gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads the TTP223 capacitive touch sensor connected via GPIO, using GPIO4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7) configured as an input with a pull‑down bias, and polls the pin with a debounce interval of approximately 50 ms to detect press and release transitions; each time a touch is detected or released the program must append a line to a file named touch_log.txt in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Detected” or “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Released”, flushing the file after every write, while verifying every driver call and printing a diagnostic message to stderr on failure, and if the log file cannot be opened the program must release all GPIO resources before exiting with a non‑zero status; additionally it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing the GPIO line, closing the log file, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the coolant flow rate from a Sensirion SLF3S‑1300F Liquid Flow Sensor attached to I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL), issuing the sensor command, waiting at least 2 ms before the first read, and then sampling once per second; each read must retrieve exactly three bytes – a 2‑byte big‑endian signed 16‑bit flow value followed by a 1‑byte CRC‑8 calculated with the documented polynomial and initial value – and the program must validate the CRC, flagging a read as an error if the CRC fails, and also verify that the converted flow rate lies within the plausible range of 0.0 to 100.0 ml/min, marking out‑of‑range values with a status of INVALID; for every successful measurement the program should log a line to a comma‑separated file named cooling_log.csv containing the timestamp, the flow rate in ml/min, the raw sensor flags, and a computed status string, writing the header “Timestamp,Flow Rate (ml/min),Status” only when the file is created for the first time, and for any I2C read failure or CRC error it must log a row with status ERROR and attempt recovery by re‑initializing the I2C handle; all driver/I2C calls and file operations must be checked for errors, and the program must handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, closes the CSV file, and terminates any driver resources on every exit path, while never using any external driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously polls three KY-033 Obstacle Avoidance Sensors (IR reflective, digital output) connected via the GPIO bus, with the left sensor on GPIO17 (BCM), the middle sensor on GPIO27 (BCM) and the right sensor on GPIO22 (BCM), sampling each sensor every 50 ms and writing each timestamped reading to a CSV file named path_log.csv using ISO‑8601 timestamps and columns “timestamp,left,middle,right” where each sensor value is recorded as 0 or 1; the program must verify that the library’s API call to open the GPIO chip succeeds, that each line can be requested as an input, and that all file I/O operations succeed, must include system headers such as <errno.h> and <stdbool.h> so it compiles without warnings under gcc ‑Wall ‑Wextra, and must handle a SIGINT signal by cleanly releasing all GPIO lines, closing the chip, flushing and closing the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that monitors a Keyes KY‑026 Flame Sensor connected via the GPIO bus, with the sensor’s digital output tied to GPIO 4 (BCM numbering), using edge‑based detection of the falling edge because the sensor is active‑low (0 indicates flame, 1 indicates no flame); the program must verify that the driver library chip and line requests succeed and must handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, printing an alert with a timestamp to stdout and appending the same event to a file named ‘flame_events.txt’ whenever a flame is detected, and it must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that simulates a touch‑activated lamp by toggling an LED whenever the TTP223 capacitive touch sensor (active‑high) reports a touch, using the GPIO bus with the sensor output connected to GPIO23 (BCM 23) and the LED to GPIO24 (BCM 24) on the /dev/gpiochip4 chip, polling line events with a 1‑second timeout and reacting only to rising‑edge events (no software debounce required), logging each touch event together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the resulting LED state to a file named touch_log.txt, checking every driver call and file operation for errors and reporting any failure to stderr, exiting with an error if the log file cannot be opened or if the GPIO chip or lines cannot be requested after cleaning up any partially initialized resources, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a flame detection safety system using the Keyes KY‑026 Flame Sensor (digital output, active‑low) and an active buzzer connected on the GPIO bus, with the sensor’s DO line wired to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) and the buzzer control line to GPIO18 (BCM, physical pin 12); the program must poll the flame sensor every 500 ms, but break both the 2‑second buzzer activation and the 500 ms poll interval into 100 ms slices so it can respond promptly to shutdown signals, detect a HIGH‑to‑LOW transition on the sensor (LOW indicates flame detected) and on each such transition log a timestamped “FLAME DETECTED” entry to a file named alert_log.txt while driving the buzzer HIGH for 2 seconds, ensuring that only the transition triggers logging and buzzing (no continuous action while the line stays LOW), write a “System started” entry at startup and a “System stopped” entry on clean shutdown, check every driver library call, file operation and system call for failure and, on any initialization error, print a diagnostic using strerror(errno) to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by turning the buzzer off, releasing the GPIO lines, closing the chip and the log file, and exiting cleanly with code 0; the source must include the headers <errno.h>, <string.h>, <time.h>, <signal.h>, <unistd.h>, <stdio.h>, <stdlib.h>, and the appropriate driver header, and it should be built with the command `gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o flame_alert flame_alert.c -lgpiod`.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a GPIO bus to read the SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor whose output is wired to GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) and toggles an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11); the program must poll GPIO4 every 10 ms, detect a LOW‑to‑HIGH transition (rising edge) from the sensor (which drives HIGH at 3.3 V when touched and LOW when released), apply a 200 ms software debounce before accepting another touch, and on each valid toggle event append a line containing a UTC ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named touch_log.txt; it must check all driver library return values and report any errors to stderr, exit with a non‑zero status if the log file cannot be opened, and if a write to the log fails, print a warning to stderr but continue running; finally, the program must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by turning off the LED, closing the log file, and calling the library’s cleanup API before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the GPIO bus to read an 8‑channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module connected on BCM pins 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 (OUT1‑OUT8) and drives an 8‑bit binary counter on GPIO 17 through GPIO 24 (bit 0 on 17, bit 7 on 24), polling the sensor lines every 10 ms after an initial 200 ms stabilization delay; on each rising edge (idle 0 V to touched 3.3 V) the program must increment the counter, wrapping from 255 to 0, immediately update the eight output pins via the driver’s bulk/config API calls, and log the event to a file named touch_log.txt in append mode using an ISO‑8601 UTC timestamp “YYYY‑MM‑DDTHH:MM:SSZ, Channel: <1‑8>, Counter: <0‑255>” while also printing to stdout “Touch on channel <N> | Counter: <V>”, checking every driver call, file open and I/O operation and reporting errors with strerror(errno); if any line request fails the program must clean up all previously acquired resources and exit non‑zero, if a driver API call fails it must print the error and exit non‑zero, if a sensor read returns an error it must log the error to stderr and skip that channel for the iteration, if an output write fails it must log the error to stderr but continue, and if opening the log file fails it must warn on stderr yet keep stdout output functional; finally the program must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by resetting all output pins to 0, releasing all driver resources, closing the chip and exiting with status 0, and it must be built with gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o touch_counter touch_counter.c -lgpiod.

#define SI1175_MEAS_RATE1_VAL 0x00
#define SI1175_ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN_VAL 0x00
#define SI1175_ALS_VIS_ADC_MISC_VAL 0x00

static volatile sig_atomic_t running = 1;
static int i2c_handle = -1;

void signal_handler(int sig) {
    (void)sig;
    running = 0;
}

int si1175_write_reg(uint8_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    int result = i2cWriteByteData(i2c_handle, reg, value);
    if (result < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error writing to register 0x%02X: %d\n", reg, result);
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

int si1175_read_reg(uint8_t reg, uint8_t *value) {
    int result = i2cReadByteData(i2c_handle, reg);
    if (result < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error reading from register 0x%02X: %d\n", reg, result);
        return -1;
    }
    *value = (uint8_t)result;
    return 0;
}

int si1175_init() {
    i2c_handle = i2cOpen(1, SI1175_ADDR, 0);
    if (i2c_handle < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error opening I2C bus: %d\n", i2c_handle);
        return -1;
    }

    uint8_t hw_key;
    if (si1175_read_reg(SI1175_REG_HW_KEY, &hw_key) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read HW_KEY register\n");
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (hw_key != SI1175_HW_KEY_VAL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Invalid HW_KEY: 0x%02X (expected 0x%02X)\n", hw_key, SI1175_HW_KEY_VAL);
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_write_reg(SI1175_REG_MEAS_RATE0, SI1175_MEAS_RATE0_VAL) != 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_write_reg(SI1175_REG_MEAS_RATE1, SI1175_MEAS_RATE1_VAL) != 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_write_reg(SI1175_REG_ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN, SI1175_ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN_VAL) != 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_write_reg(SI1175_REG_ALS_VIS_ADC_MISC, SI1175_ALS_VIS_ADC_MISC_VAL) != 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

int si1175_read_raw_data(uint16_t *raw_data) {
    uint8_t lsb, msb;

    if (si1175_read_reg(SI1175_REG_ALS_VIS_DATA0, &lsb) != 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_read_reg(SI1175_REG_ALS_VIS_DATA1, &msb) != 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    *raw_data = ((uint16_t)msb << 8) | lsb;
    return 0;
}

int main() {
    struct sigaction sa;
    sa.sa_handler = signal_handler;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = 0;
    sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL);
    sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL);

    if (si1175_init() != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Sensor initialization failed. Exiting.\n");
        return 1;
    }

    printf("Si1175 sensor initialized successfully. Reading data...\n");

    while (running) {
        uint16_t raw_data;
        if (si1175_read_raw_data(&raw_data) == 0) {
            printf("Raw ALS Data: %u\n", raw_data);
        } else {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read raw ALS data. Retrying...\n");
        }
        gpioDelay(100000); // 100ms delay
    }

    printf("\nExiting gracefully...\n");
    if (i2c_handle >= 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
    }
    return 0;
}

static volatile sig_atomic_t running = 1;
static int i2c_handle = -1;

void signal_handler(int sig) {
    (void)sig;
    running = 0;
}

int si1175_write_reg(uint8_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    int result = i2cWriteByteData(i2c_handle, reg, value);
    if (result < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error writing to register 0x%02X: %d\n", reg, result);
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

int si1175_read_reg(uint8_t reg, uint8_t *value) {
    int result = i2cReadByteData(i2c_handle, reg);
    if (result < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error reading from register 0x%02X: %d\n", reg, result);
        return -1;
    }
    *value = (uint8_t)result;
    return 0;
}

int si1175_init() {
    i2c_handle = i2cOpen(1, SI1175_ADDR, 0);
    if (i2c_handle < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error opening I2C bus: %d\n", i2c_handle);
        return -1;
    }

    uint8_t hw_key;
    if (si1175_read_reg(SI1175_REG_HW_KEY, &hw_key) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read HW_KEY register\n");
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (hw_key != SI1175_HW_KEY_VAL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Invalid HW_KEY: 0x%02X (expected 0x%02X)\n", hw_key, SI1175_HW_KEY_VAL);
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_write_reg(SI1175_REG_MEAS_RATE0, SI1175_MEAS_RATE0_VAL) != 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_write_reg(SI1175_REG_MEAS_RATE1, SI1175_MEAS_RATE1_VAL) != 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_write_reg(SI1175_REG_ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN, SI1175_ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN_VAL) != 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_write_reg(SI1175_REG_ALS_VIS_ADC_MISC, SI1175_ALS_VIS_ADC_MISC_VAL) != 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        i2c_handle = -1;
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

int si1175_read_raw_data(uint16_t *raw_data) {
    uint8_t lsb, msb;

    if (si1175_read_reg(SI1175_REG_ALS_VIS_DATA0, &lsb) != 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    if (si1175_read_reg(SI1175_REG_ALS_VIS_DATA1, &msb) != 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    *raw_data = ((uint16_t)msb << 8) | lsb;
    return 0;
}

int main() {
    struct sigaction sa;
    sa.sa_handler = signal_handler;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = 0;
    sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL);
    sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL);

    if (si1175_init() != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Sensor initialization failed. Exiting.\n");
        return 1;
    }

    printf("Si1175 sensor initialized successfully. Reading data...\n");

    while (running) {
        uint16_t raw_data;
        if (si1175_read_raw_data(&raw_data) == 0) {
            printf("Raw ALS Data: %u\n", raw_data);
        } else {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read raw ALS data. Retrying...\n");
        }
        gpioDelay(100000); // 100ms delay
    }

    printf("\nExiting gracefully...\n");
    if (i2c_handle >= 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
    }
    return 0;
}

/*
 * ADIS16488A IMU reader for Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
 * SPI0 CE0 (GPIO8), 1 MHz, mode 3 (CPOL=1, CPHA=1)
 * Logs timestamped gyro/accel data to imu_data.csv
 *
 * Build: gcc -O2 -Wall -o imu_reader imu_reader.c
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define SPI_CHANNEL    0          /* CE0 */
#define SPI_SPEED      1000000    /* 1 MHz */
#define SPI_FLAGS      0          /* Mode 3, active-low CE */
#define STALL_US       40         /* >= 40 us between request and data */
#define SAMPLE_US      100000     /* 100 ms between samples */
#define LOG_FILE       "imu_data.csv"
#define MAX_RETRIES    3

/* ADIS16488A register addresses (MSB = 0) */
#define REG_XGYRO_OUT  0x00
#define REG_YGYRO_OUT  0x01
#define REG_ZGYRO_OUT  0x02
#define REG_XACCEL_OUT 0x03
#define REG_YACCEL_OUT 0x04

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that communicates with an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI bus 0 using chip‑select CS0 on GPIO8 (BCM) in SPI mode 3 with a maximum clock of 1 MHz, reads the gyroscope and accelerometer registers using the single‑register read protocol (send the 8‑bit register address with bit 7 set in the first 16‑bit SPI cycle and capture the 16‑bit data response in the second cycle), applies the gyro scale of 0.02 dps/LSB and accel scale of 0.00025 g/LSB, and logs the six values (gyroscope X, Y, Z and accelerometer X, Y, Z) to the console every 100 ms; the program must include robust error handling for SPI initialization, ioctl transfers, and data reads, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly release resources by closing the SPI device file and the driver library chip before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses an IR receiver such as the TSOP38238 connected to GPIO17 (BCM) to decode NEC infrared remote signals and report the decoded commands both to syslog and to an MQTT broker at localhost on port 1883 using the topic ir/decoded, publishing the command as a JSON object; the program must register an alert callback on the falling edge of the GPIO to capture pulse timings, interpret the NEC frame consisting of a 9 ms mark followed by a 4.5 ms space header, 560 µs marks for each bit, a 1690 µs space for logic‑1 and a 560 µs space for logic‑0, decode the full 32‑bit frame, validate the command against its inverted copy while allowing extended NEC frames that omit inverted‑address validation, check driver initialization and GPIO setup failures, guard against pulse‑buffer overflow, verify the NEC checksum, initialize the MQTT client once at startup and invoke the network loop in the main loop, and ensure clean release of all resources—including the driver, MQTT client, and syslog—when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient light from four BH1750FVI sensors attached to I2C‑1, waiting 180 ms after each start‑conversion command, and repeats this acquisition loop once per second; for each sensor the program must issue an ioctl(I2C_SLAVE, addr) before any transaction, may use a single /dev/i2c-1 descriptor or one per sensor, and must not rely on any external driver library, handling any open, address‑set, write, read or partial‑read failure by inserting a NaN value for that sensor while continuing with the others; after gathering the lux values it must broadcast a UDP multicast packet to 239.255.255.250:5005 containing a semicolon‑separated list of sensor_id,lux pairs such as 1,120.5;2,85.0;3,210.5;4,45.0, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a termination flag so the loop can exit cleanly, ensuring that all file descriptors for I2C and the UDP socket are closed on every exit path.

static int i2c_write_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    uint8_t buf[2] = { reg, value };
    if (write(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write to reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *value) {
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, value, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg16(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint16_t *value) {
    uint8_t buf[2];
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read16 from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    *value = (uint16_t)buf[0] | ((uint16_t)buf[1] << 8);
    return 0;
}

static int as7341_init(int fd) {
    uint8_t id = 0;
    if (i2c_read_reg8(fd, AS7341_ID, &id) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read AS7341 ID register.\n");
        return -1;
    }
    if (id != AS7341_ID_EXPECTED) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Unexpected AS7341 ID: 0x%02X (expected 0x%02X).\n", id, AS7341_ID_EXPECTED);
        return -1;
    }

    /* Power on */
    if (i2c_write_reg8(fd, AS7341_ENABLE, 0x01) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    usleep(10000); /* 10 ms settle */

    /* Enable spectral measurement */
    if (i2c_write_reg8(fd, AS7341_ENABLE, 0x03) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    usleep(10000); /* 10 ms settle */

    /* Configure SMUX: F1-F8, Clear, NIR */
    if (i2c_write_reg8(fd, AS7341_CFG6, 0x00) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

static int as7341_read_spectral(int fd, uint16_t *data) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        if (i2c_read_reg16(fd, AS7341_DATA0 + i * 2, &data[i]) < 0) {
            return -1;
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

static float calculate_lux(const uint16_t *data) {
    float lux = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        lux += (float)data[i];
    }
    return lux;
}

static int i2c_write_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    uint8_t buf[2] = { reg, value };
    if (write(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write to reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *value) {
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, value, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg16(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint16_t *value) {
    uint8_t buf[2];
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (reg select 0x%02X) failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read16 from reg 0x%02X failed: %s\n", reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    *value = (uint16_t)buf[0] | ((uint16_t)buf[1] << 8);
    return 0;
}

static int as7341_init(int fd) {
    uint8_t id = 0;
    if (i2c_read_reg8(fd, AS7341_ID, &id) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read AS7341 ID register.\n");
        return -1;
    }
    if (id != AS7341_ID_EXPECTED) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Unexpected AS7341 ID: 0x%02X (expected 0x%02X).\n", id, AS7341_ID_EXPECTED);
        return -1;
    }

    /* Power on */
    if (i2c_write_reg8(fd, AS7341_ENABLE, 0x01) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    usleep(10000); /* 10 ms settle */

    /* Enable spectral measurement */
    if (i2c_write_reg8(fd, AS7341_ENABLE, 0x03) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    usleep(10000); /* 10 ms settle */

    /* Configure SMUX: F1-F8, Clear, NIR */
    if (i2c_write_reg8(fd, AS7341_CFG6, 0x00) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

            return -1;
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

    float lux = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        lux += (float)data[i];
    }
    return lux;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads tri‑axial acceleration data from an Omron D7S seismic sensor over the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) and logs the timestamped X, Y, Z values in g to a CSV file named seismic_data.csv by default, with columns timestamp,x_g,y_g,z_g, while also writing any error messages with timestamps to seismic_error.log; the program must accept a command‑line option ‑a to specify the I2C address (defaulting to the documented value), ‑i to set the sampling interval in seconds (default 1 s), and ‑f to set the output filename (default seismic_data.csv), perform reads at the configured interval, check every I2C read/write return value, retry transient failures up to three times with a 10 ms backoff, detect sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the I2C file descriptor and flushing and closing the CSV file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the ambient light from a BH1750 light sensor attached to the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) once every second, converts the 16‑bit big‑endian raw value to a floating‑point lux value, and broadcasts that value as a floating‑point string via UDP multicast to 239.255.255.250:5000 with a TTL of 1; the program must check every I2C write and read operation for failure, and if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs it should print an error message and retry after one second, and it must install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the socket before exiting, using only the Linux I2C ioctl interface and standard POSIX sockets, and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/ttyS0) at 921600 baud, reads the sensor’s data stream, synchronizes on the documented 8‑byte little‑endian magic word, validates each TLV payload, extracts the range (in meters) and velocity (in meters per second) for every detected object, and appends rows to a file named radar_data.csv with the columns timestamp, object_index, range_m, velocity_mps; the program must check every UART read, handle partial reads and buffer overflows gracefully, skip malformed frames, log any errors to stderr without crashing, and on all exit paths including SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly release resources by closing the UART using the provided driver library, flushing and closing the CSV file, and invoking the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit OS that periodically reads range‑detection data from a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/serial0, GPIO14/GPIO15 BCM pins as TXD/RXD) at 115200 baud, 8N1, using a 0.5 second inter‑byte timeout and a select() call with a 2‑second timeout to detect sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions; the program must open and configure the UART in non‑canonical mode, accumulate partial reads into a line buffer, parse only complete newline‑terminated ASCII lines of the form `<unix_timestamp_seconds>,<range_meters>\n`, and for each valid detection log to stdout exactly as “Timestamp: YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Range: X.XX meters”, while checking the result of every system call (open, tcgetattr, tcsetattr, read, select, strdup) and printing errno‑based diagnostics on failure, and must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure a graceful shutdown that closes the UART on all exit paths, using only standard POSIX C libraries such as stdio, stdlib, string, fcntl, unistd, errno, sys/select, signal, and time.
